pages.page_summary: Nick Carraway sits at his writing desk and begins the manuscript of this story; as he writes, he recalls his father's old counsel about judgement, reflects on how that habit shaped his college years and his recent return from the East, and finally names the one exception to his disillusion—Gatsby, glimpsed as a distant silhouette.

panels.caption: I lived at West Egg — the less fashionable of the two, a most superficial tag for a bizarre and not a little sinister contrast. My house sat at the very tip, squeezed between two huge places that rented for twelve or fifteen thousand a season. The one on my right was a factual imitation of some Hôtel de Ville in Normandy — tower, marble pool, forty acres of lawn. It was Gatsby's mansion. Or, since I didn't yet know Mr. Gatsby, a mansion inhabited by a gentleman of that name.
